Materials In 45 sentences sets with optionally transitive verbs (24 from Christianson et al. (2001), 21 crafted for this study), we manipulated the structure of the sentence (GP or non-GP) and the plausibility of the noun as the verb's object (plausible or implausible), as exemplified in (4). We also created 24 additional sets with reflexive/unaccusative verbs (12 from Christianson et al. (2001) and 12 crafted for this study) in plausible sentences, manipulating structure (GP/non-GP), as exemplified in (5).

4. (a) GP, plausible: While the man hunted the deer ran into the woods.   
(b) Non-GP, plausible: The deer ran into the woods while the man hunted.   
(c) GP, implausible: While the man hunted the child ran into the woods.   
(d) Non-GP, implausible: The child ran into the woods while the man hunted.

5. (a) GP, reflexive: While the boy washed the dog barked loudly.   
(b) Non-GP, reflexive: The dog barked loudly while the boy washed.

To construct materials for the plausibility manipulation (hypothesis 2), we use insights from Amouyal et al. (2024), and let GPT-4 rate sentence plausibility on a 1 to 7 scale. We select pairs where the plausible sentence had a rating of at least 3 points higher than its implausible counterpart. For the second part of hypothesis 3, we assessed each optionally-transitive verb's bias by its proportion of transitive usage on Wikipedia. Our verbs' bias ranges from 0.102 ("sail") to 0.775 ("explore"). Appendix A lists the full estimated verb biases, and all the sentences are in Appendix B.

For each sentence, we ask one of two questions:

1. Simple: "Did the deer run into the woods?"   
2. $GP$ : "Did the man hunt the deer?"

The simple question probes the basic understanding of the sentence, whereas the GP question targets the potential misinterpretation.

Procedure Native English speakers were recruited via the Prolific platform. Sentences were displayed word-by-word, with each word shown for 400ms and a 100ms blank screen between words. After the sentence, the comprehension question was presented for 5 seconds. If unanswered within this time, the response was marked as incorrect. Participants completed two practice items, followed by one experimental sentence and one question. The single-trial design prevents fatigue (Christianson et al., 2022) and learning effects (Fine et al., 2013). Each of the 456 sentence-question pairs $(45\mathrm{x}4\mathrm{x}2 + 24\mathrm{x}2\mathrm{x}2)$ was shown to 10 participants. The average completion time was 1:50 minutes, and participants were compensated with $0.30\text{£}$ , equivalent to $9.64\text{£}$ per hour. The experiment was approved by the Ethics Committee at Tel-Aviv University.

To replicate the experiment with LLMs, we used few-shot prompting, where each example includes a sentence, a question, and the correct answer. The examples did not contain GP structures, to prevent in-context learning of the structure. Each model was prompted 8 times, using two system prompts and four example orderings. We extract the probabilities of the correct and incorrect answers tokens, averaging these across the 8 prompts. Appendix E shows an example prompt.

Models We test models from different families, sizes and training checkpoints:

1. GPT family (OpenAI, 2023): GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1-preview, o1-mini.   
2. Llama-3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024): All models from the Llama-3 family (Llama-3.2 and Llama-3.1) available on HuggingFace.<sup>3</sup>   
3. Qwen-2.5 (Yang et al., 2024; Qwen Team, 2024): All Qwen-2.5 models on Hugging-Face except models of size 0.5b.   
4. Gemma-2 (Team et al., 2024): All Gemma-2 models on HuggingFace.   
5. Olmo (Groeneveld et al., 2024): 15 Olmo-1b and Olmo-7b checkpoints along training.

# When the LM misunderstood the human chuckled: Analyzing garden path effects in humans and language models

Samuel Joseph Amouyal $^{\lambda}$ Aya Meltzer-Asscher $^{\dagger,\star}$ Jonathan Berant $^{\lambda}$

$\lambda$ Blavatnik School of Computer Science, Tel Aviv University, Israel

† Department of Linguistics, Tel Aviv University, Israel

{samuel.amouyal,从业者}.cs.tau.ac.il

ameltzer@tauex.tau.ac.il

# Abstract

Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown human-like abilities in many language tasks, sparking interest in comparing LLMs' and humans' language processing. In this paper, we try to answer two questions: 1. What makes garden-path sentences hard to understand for humans? 2. Do the same reasons make garden-path sentences hard for LLMs as well? Based on psycholinguistic research, we formulate hypotheses on why garden-path sentences, and test these hypotheses using comprehension questions on human participants and a large suite of LLMs using comprehension questions. Our findings reveal that both LLMs and humans struggle with specific syntactic complexities, with some models showing high correlation with human comprehension. To complement our findings, we test LLM comprehension of garden-path constructions with paraphrasing and text-to-image generation tasks, and find that the results mirror the comprehension question results, further validating our findings on LLM understanding of these constructions.

# 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown high proficiency in language comprehension and generation, demonstrating performance that matches and sometimes surpasses human capabilities across a range of tasks (OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Almazrouei et al., 2023; Grattafori et al., 2024; Gemini, 2024). This has sparked a line of research focused on comparing sentence-processing mechanisms in humans and LLMs. Within this research, some studies have found correlations between LLM activations and brain activations during the processing of identical sentences (Cacheteux and King, 2022; Schrimpf et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2024). Others have demonstrated that LLMs can be used to predict human linguistic behavior metrics (such as reading time,

While LLMs mostly succeed where humans succeed, less is known about whether LLMs fail where humans fail. In psycholinguistic research, a well-studied type of sentences where humans systematically have comprehension difficulty is Garden Path (GP) structures (Ferreira and Henderson, 1990; Trueswell et al., 1993; Garnsey et al., 1997). GP sentences are temporarily structurally ambiguous, and their beginning often leads readers to misconstrue their parse. In this paper, we focus on one type of GP sentences, exemplified in (1)-(2). In (1), readers initially misanalyze "the dog" as the object of "washed", although in the final, correct structure, "the dog" is the subject of "barked", and "washed" has no object.

Christianson et al. (2001) used comprehension questions and found that comprehension is poorer for GP sentences like (1) compared to semantically equivalent non-GP sentences like (2). Specifically, the initial interpretation, where the post-verbal NP is analyzed as the object of the first verb (i.e The boy washed the dog), lingers, while the NP is also analyzed as the subject of the following verb (see also Christianson et al. (2006)). Patson et al. (2009) similarly showed that when participants were tasked with paraphrasing GP sentences, they often gave paraphrases such as "The boy washed the dog and the dog barked" for (1).

Some prior studies examined how LLMs handle GP sentences. Arehalli et al. (2022) found that LLM-based metrics significantly underestimate the processing difficulties (measured using reading times) that humans face with GP sentences. Hanna and Mueller (2024) found that LMs encode multiple p

Hanna and Mueller (2024) found that LMs encode multiple parses of GP sentences, which does not straightforwardly align with human performance. Irwin et al. (2023) reported that BERT misinterprets GP sentences, although with different error patterns than humans. In contrast, Li et al. (2024) observed that four LLMs make parsing errors akin to human errors. Despite these findings, gaps remain in existing research. First, it remains unclear whether the same aspects of GP structures cause processing difficulties in humans and LLMs. Second, the breadth of LLM families considered has been limited thus far. Lastly, the comparison between humans and LLMs has been mostly carried out through indirect measures, where e.g. human reading times are correlated with LLM uncertainty (Wilcox et al., 2022; Rego et al., 2024; Sun and Wang, 2024), whereas a comparison on the same task could be more revealing. In this study, we explore object/subject GP sentences (similar to (1)) with humans and LLMs, with both responding to exactly the same task, namely, a comprehension question about the sentence (e.g., "Did the boy wash the dog?"). We present three (non-mutually exclusive) hypotheses regarding the challenges posed by GP sentences: (a) Misinterpretation of the noun phrase as the object of the verb arises due to the difficulty of syntactic reanalysis; (b) Misinterpretation arises since the noun phrase is a plausible object for the verb (e.g., boys tend to wash dogs); (c) Misinterpretation arises since transitive verbs ("hunt") entail some object. Reflexive ("wash") or unaccusative ("drop") verbs, which are interpreted with no direct object, will give rise to less misinterpretation. We test our hypotheses on sets of sentences instantiating the various manipulations (see Table 1) and tested comprehension in humans and LLMs. Our human results (Fig. 1, left) provide evidence for all three hypotheses. Accuracy is lower (i) when reanalysis is needed (i.e. in GP compared to non-GP structures), (ii) when the noun is a plausible (compared to implausible) object for the verb, and (iii) when the verb is transitive, entailing an object, compared to reflexive/unaccusative. Examining multiple models within the same families reveals that stronger models tend to display greater similarity to human behavior, as shown in Figure 1 (right) for Gemma-2-9B. Finally, we validate our results for LLMs with two additional sentence comprehension tasks – paraphrasing and image generation. Both tasks produced results akin to the comprehension questions task. We release our data, resuluts and relevant codebase at: https://github.com/samsam3232/gardenpath_humans_11m. # 2 What Makes Object/Subject Garden-Path Sentences Hard? Object/subject garden-path sentences, like (1), include an embedded verb ("wash") followed by a noun phrase ("the dog") and the main verb ("barked"). These sentences cause processing difficulties, leading to slower reading—especially at the main verb—and impaired comprehension (Frazier and Rayner, 1982; Arehalli et al., 2022; Christianson et al., 2001, 2006; Staub, 2007). In sentence (1), "the dog" will often be mistakenly interpreted as the object of "wash", prompting incorrect answers like "Yes" to the question "Did the child wash the dog?". This happens even though in the final structure of the sentence, "the dog" is not an object of "washed". Several (non-mutually exclusive) hypotheses can explain the misinterpretation described above, as summarized in Table 1. Note that the accurate answer to the question above is "Not necessarily". It is a possible interpretation of the sentence, and may be inferred from it, but it is not entailed from the sentence. This is always the case in sentences with optionally transitive verbs such as "hunt". For sentences with reflexive or unaccusative verbs such as (1) above, "While the boy washed the dog barked", the correct answer for "Did the boy wash the dog?" is unambiguously "No". In our experiments, as in previous experiments, we consider "yes" to be a wrong answer in all sentences, whereas "no" is considered the right answer.

Hypothesis 1: The GP syntax is hard. This hypothesis suggests that misinterpretation occurs because during incremental processing, the postverbal noun phrase ("the deer") is first attached as the object of the verb, requiring reanalysis when the second verb is encountered. Often, the reanalysis is not complete, and the initial interpretation lingers. According to this, reordering the clauses (see Table 1) should improve accuracy by preventing initial misattachment.

Hypothesis 2: Readers attach the noun to the first verb when the noun is a plausible object for it. According to this hypothesis, readers interpret a noun as an object of a verb in the sentence whenever this is semantically plausible, regardless of structural position. If the noun is an implausi

ble direct object, it will not be interpreted as such, improving accuracy (see Table 1).

Hypothesis 3: Readers aim for maximal interpretation of verb arguments. According to this hypothesis, optionally transitive verbs (such as "hunt") need objects for full interpretation, so available nouns are taken to fulfill this role. In contrast, alternating reflexive ("wash") and unaccusative verbs ("drop") allow complete interpretation intransitively, without an object (e.g., The boy washed, The ball dropped). Thus, such verbs will not attach the noun as their object, and will thus allow more accurate interpretation than optionally transitive verbs (see Table 1). As for the optionally transitive verbs, it can also be hypothesized that the tendency to attach an object to them depends on the verb's transitivity bias (the probability that the verb appears with a direct object). According to this hypothesis, verbs with a lower bias (e.g., "walk") should lead to better accuracy compared to those with a higher bias (e.g., "explore"), as the noun is less likely to be considered as their object.

As mentioned earlier, prior studies already investigated human sentence comprehension of object/subject garden-path sentences (Christianson et al., 2001, 2006). The sentences they evaluated were GP and non-GP sentences in the plausible and reflexive setups. The overall trends (GP being harder than non-GP, and optionally transitive being harder than reflexive) were similar in this line of work. However, the accuracy they reported was higher than the one we found in our experiment (e.g., the accuracy of non-GP reflexive sentences was $86\%$ ). We conjecture that this is due to our experimental setup, where we ran our experiment in a single-trial setup vs. the multi-trial setup in previous experiments, where participants can adapt to the task. This highlights the importance of the single-trial setup, which prevents this learning effect. The full results from (Christianson et al., 2001, 2006) can be found in Appendix D.

# 4 LLMs Performance

We now analyze the performance of LLMs on our different experimental conditions.

# 4.1 Methodology

To replicate the experiment with LLMs, we used few-shot prompting, where each example includes a sentence, a question, and the correct answer. The examples did not contain GP structures, to prevent in-context learning of the structure. Each model was prompted 8 times, using two system prompts and four example orderings. We extract the probabilities of the correct and incorrect answers tokens, averaging these across the 8 prompts. Appendix E shows an example prompt.

# 7 Conclusion

This study explores similarities between human and LLM sentence processing. By focusing on comprehension of garden-path sentences, known for their syntactic complexity and inherent challenges for human processing, we studied whether LLMs have similar difficulties to humans. Our findings demonstrate that humans and LLMs struggle with similar syntactic structures, and notably, some LLMs approximate human behavior quite closely, as indicated by strong correlation

Our approach not only adds a novel dimension to the evaluation of LLMs but also opens up possibilities for utilizing these models to gain deeper insights into human linguistic processing.

# Limitations

In our study, we evaluated reading comprehension across a wide array of LLMs. However, the latest state-of-the-art models appeared too late to be incorporated into this version of our paper. Assessing their understanding of our sets would be interesting for a future version of this paper. Additionally, our focus was limited to measuring reading comprehension on Subject/Object GP sentences. Exploring LLMs' comprehension of other types of GP sentences would also be interesting. Finally, we did not collect data on metrics beyond reading comprehension, such as eye gaze or reading time, in our experiments. Gathering such metrics and analyzing their correlation with sentence comprehension could provide valuable insights.

# G Error analyses

We performed the following analyses to explain human errors, without success.

1. Manual analysis: we tried to look at the sentences that were more challenging for humans and looked for any surface difference. We did not see any.

2. Asking o1-pro: we took sentences on which 8 out of 10 (or more) participants answered correctly and sentences on which 2 out of 10 (or less) participants answered correctly and asked o1-pro if it saw any difference. It did not see any notable difference.

3. Correlating various LLM probability related metrics: we tried to correlate various LLM related metrics (perplexity of the LLM on the sentence, surprisal of the disambiguation word, 'ran' in the sentence "While the man hunted the deer ran into the woods.") with the average correctness of human participants. Sadly, this did not bear fruit either (Kendall tau correlation of -0.04 for the perplexity and 0.01 for the surprisal of disambiguation word for Gemma-2-9b).

4. Correlating attention related metrics: we tried to correlate some basic attention metric to the average correctness of human participants. In the sentence, "While the man hunted the deer ran into the woods," we subtracted the attention value between ('ran',

'deer') to the attention value between ('deer', 'hunted'). A positive coefficient means that there is more attention on the correct interpretation than on the incorrect. For each layer, we averaged this value across the attention heads. The highest Kendall-tau correlation between a metric and human average correctness (0.19 with the attention from layer 19 of Gemma-2-2b) is still quite low.
